newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Holbrooke, Milosevic meet to discuss Balkan issues.
newsitem.headline: Holbrooke, Milosevic meet to discuss Balkan issues.

text.p: U.S. envoy Richard Holbrooke meets Yugoslav President Slobodan Milosevic on Friday in the next stage of his efforts to revive the stalled Bosnian peace process.
Holbrooke, architect of the Dayton accords that halted four years of wars in Bosnia and Croatia, is in the region to lean on political leaders in Bosnia, Croatia and Yugoslavia.
Holbrooke scored a major victory for U.S. diplomacy earlier on Friday when he forged an accord among recalcitrant Bosnian leaders over the distribution of ambassadorial posts.
It is Holbrooke's first visit to the region since he negotiated a deal last year that forced indicted war criminal Radovan Karadzic to step down as Bosnian Serb president.
Under the deal which was also signed by his former patron, Milosevic, Karadzic was supposed to stay out of politics.
One year later, Karadzic and his allies persist in attempting to circumvent the 1995 Dayton accords.
Bosnian Serb President Biljana Plavsic has publicly accused them of plundering the territory through vast smuggling rackets and making the country their personal fiefdom.
Diplomats said Holbrooke would threaten Milosevic with economic sanctions unless he abides by his Dayton commitments, which include handing over Karadzic and other war criminals.
Diplomats said Milosevic was toughening his position, feeling he was not being rewarded enough by the international community for his cooperation in engineering the peace accords.
"It takes one tough guy to know another," a diplomat said
Holbrooke won world plaudits for securing an agreement at Dayton, where Milosevic showed his willingness to cooperate with the U.S. envoy.
In return Milosevic shed his image as a Serbian autocrat widely blamed for starting the Balkan wars of the early 1990s and was praised as a peace-maker.
Western envoys acknowledge Milosevic is a master of brinksmanship in negotiations.
Washington has maintained diplomatic and financial sanctions against Yugoslavia to bar it from receiving the foreign funds it desperately needs to restart its moribund economy.
Diplomats say Bosnia will not be the only item on the genda when Holbrooke meets Milosevic.

Milosevic will also face tough questioning about Serbia's handling of human rights in its mostly-Albanian populated province of Kosovo, the freedom of the media in Serbia, and the slow pace of democracy and economic reforms.

The diplomats said time and money were running out for the Yugoslav economy as the government struggled hard to maintain order and feed the 11-million strong population, a third of which was living in poverty.
"Holbrooke is bringing a bagful of carrots and sticks. Its up to Milosevic to chose which he would rather have," one diplomat said.

Diplomats said one reason why Holbrooke was in Belgrade was that other negotiatiors "had enough with Milosevic telling them how they were not present in Dayton so could not really know what was said and agreed."
Holbrooke is a seasoned diplomat known in Washington for his ambition and a sharp tongue and wit to match.
His active role and unswerving dedication to negotiating a peace deal prompted some to call him, much to his pleasure, as "The Kissinger of the Balkans".
Outspoken and unabashed in the endless stream of media interviews he has given, Holbrooke once described Milosevic as "not a nice man."
Milosevic has been the dominant figure in Yugoslav politics since the breakup of the old six-member Balkan federation in 1991-92 which plunged Bosnia and Croatia into war.
His takeover last month of the Yugoslav presidency, hitherto a relatively ceremonial post, is seen as a manoeuvre to remain a power broker in the the Balkans.
